title: Levinas
tradition: The ethics of the Other and the philosophy of dialogue
keyWorks: E. Levinas, Time and the Other (1947)
E. Levinas, Otherwise than Being, or Beyond Essence (1974)
summary: Emmanuel Levinas was a French philosopher for whom the central question was not "what is being?" but "how do I respond to another person?" He called ethics "first philosophy": the encounter with the other, with their "face", comes before any theory. Beside him here stands Martin Buber, author of I and Thou, for whom real life is encounter.
onEmotions: Levinas said little about feelings as inner states — he was interested in how feelings open us to the other. He stressed "sensibility" in the sense of vulnerability: we are capable of being affected, and this is exactly what makes responsibility and closeness possible. From this point of view, many of our experiences are responses to an encounter or to its absence. Buber distinguished the "I–Thou" relation, in which we meet the other as a whole, from "I–It", in which we deal with them as an object. Seen this way, a feeling is not only something happening "in me" but also something happening "between".

anxiety.text: Levinas believed that what leads us out of the most muffled anxiety is not an effort of will but another person's face turned towards us. If you feel anxious now, this thought may prove unexpectedly practical. In his early book Existence and Existents (1947), Levinas described an experience he called the "il y a" — "there is": impersonal, anonymous being that hums like the silence of a sleepless night, when there is nothing to hold on to — no object, no meaning. He called it "horror" before faceless being, and many people know the description from nights of insomnia. What matters is that, for Levinas, the way out of this state is not to close in on yourself even more, but the relation to another person: the other pulls us out of our confinement in our own existence. Then anxiety can be eased not only by inner work but also by simply turning to someone nearby — a question, a glance, a conversation.
anxiety.practice: Ask someone today, "How are you?" — and listen to the answer all the way through, looking at their face. Notice what happens to your anxiety while you listen.

fear.text: Levinas thought that fearing for yourself and fearing for someone else are two different fears, and the second may be the most human thing in us. Fear protects what is dear to you. Heidegger, with whom Levinas studied and later argued, linked a person's deepest anxiety to their own mortality. Levinas, in his essay "Ethics as First Philosophy", spoke instead of "fear for the other" — the fact that a person can be afraid not only for themselves but for someone else, for their vulnerability. Such fear is not weakness but a sign of responsibility: you feel that the other's fate matters to you. If your fear is for someone, Levinas would see in it ethics at work, not mere worry. And if it is for yourself, it reminds you that you too are vulnerable — and in this you are like everyone else.
fear.practice: Ask yourself: whom am I afraid for right now — myself or someone else? If someone else, picture their face and silently say: "Here I am."

sadness.text: A fortress or an open door? Levinas had no doubt: a person is not a fortress but a being that can be hurt, touched, moved. Your sadness needs no justification: it says that something has touched you. Levinas gave enormous weight to "sensibility" — not in the sense of sensuality, but in the sense of openness, of being woundable. In his late book Otherwise than Being (1974), he described this vulnerability as "a passivity more passive than all passivity": we are always already open to the world and to others — before we have decided to be. If so, sadness is not a malfunction but an expression of the same woundability that makes compassion and love possible. If you were invulnerable, you could not respond to others either.
sadness.practice: Place your palm where you feel the sadness in your body and silently say: "Something has touched me." For Levinas, woundability is not a defect but the beginning of response.

grief.text: In his lectures God, Death, and Time (1975–1976), Levinas offered an unfamiliar thought: we come to know death not by reflecting on our own but when another departs. So grief concerns not only you but also the one who is no longer beside you — the one you can no longer answer. It needs time, and it keeps no correct schedule. Levinas linked this experience to a responsibility that does not end with the other's life. In this light, your mourning is a continuation of the relationship, not its end. Remembering, telling stories about the one who is gone, caring for what was dear to them — these are forms of the same faithfulness.
grief.practice: Today, make one small gesture in honour of the one who is gone — something that was dear to them: water their plant, play their music. For Levinas, this is a response that continues the relationship.

loneliness.text: "One can share everything with another except existence itself," Levinas said in his lectures Time and the Other (1947): in this sense each of us is unique and alone. If you feel lonely now, Levinas would not play down how heavy that is. But Levinas does not stop there. He sees the way out in the relation to the Other, who does not dissolve into us or become our reflection. Martin Buber said something similar in I and Thou (1923): a person becomes themselves in real encounter, where the other is not a function or a means but a "Thou". So loneliness is not a final fact but a longing for encounter — which can happen even in a brief moment of genuine attention.
loneliness.practice: Step outside for a little while and look at one tree the way Buber suggested: not as an object but as a "Thou" standing before you. Stay with it for a minute.

anger.text: "Do not harm me" — this, for Levinas, is what another person's face says before any words: not their appearance but their very defencelessness addresses us. Anger is a living feeling, and it often speaks of a crossed boundary or an injustice. This means anger is the moment when the other becomes merely an obstacle and we stop seeing their face. Levinas does not demand that you not be angry. But he reminds us that even the one who angered us remains a vulnerable human being. In Buber's terms, in anger a "Thou" easily turns into an "It". Admitting your anger is honest; keeping the person behind the act in view means keeping the possibility of finding words rather than a blow.
anger.practice: Before you reply, take three slow out-breaths and picture this person's face tired or bewildered. The anger won't vanish, but different words will come.

shame.text: In 1935 the young Levinas described shame as the impossibility of hiding from yourself: in shame we are as if chained to our own existence. It is painful, and everyone knows it. In Totality and Infinity (1961), shame takes on another meaning: the encounter with another person calls into question my self-assurance, my habit of treating the world as mine. Such shame is the beginning of conscience, not humiliation. This is an important distinction: there is a shame that paralyses and makes you want to disappear, and there is a shame that opens you to the other. So you can ask which one you are feeling now — and notice that the second does not humiliate but makes you more human.
shame.practice: Ask yourself: is this shame asking me to hide — or to turn towards someone else? If the second, take one step towards them: a word, a question, an apology.

guilt.text: When Levinas spoke of where ethics begins, he reached for two words from the Bible: "Here I am." Guilt can be heavy, and it is important not to confuse it with a verdict on yourself. Levinas built his ethics on responsibility: another person addresses me, and I am called to respond — even before I have decided anything. This responsibility, for Levinas, is asymmetrical: I do not expect the other to do the same for me. It sounds demanding, but there is an important nuance: responsibility in Levinas is a turning towards the other, not self-flagellation. For Levinas, guilt which shuts a person up in themselves in fact turns them away from the other. Responsibility asks instead: what can I do now? So it helps to turn guilt into a question about action — apologising, making amends, taking care — rather than carrying it like a stone.
guilt.practice: Replace the question "how bad am I?" with "what can I do for the other now?" — and write down one small step, if there is one.

envy.text: Levinas would probably see in envy a small error of vision: we take the other for someone "just like me", only luckier. It is an unpleasant but entirely human feeling. Levinas insisted, however, that the other is not my reflection or a "second self" (alter ego) but someone radically different, who cannot be reduced to my measures. Thinking that reduces everything to a common denominator he called "totality". Envy is a small totality: it puts us and the other on the same scale. To see in the other not a rival on the same ladder but a separate, unfathomable life with its own difficulties is to loosen envy a little, without denying it.
envy.practice: Imagine one difficulty in the life of the person you envy — one you know nothing about. Levinas would say: this is how they become a face again, not a line in a ranking.

emptiness.text: Bread, air, sunlight, work — in Totality and Infinity Levinas began his description of human life not with lofty ideas but with simply "living from" things. If you feel empty inside, it does not mean you are an "empty" person. He called this "enjoyment" — not luxury, but the basic taste of life in which we first become ourselves. Apathy, then, is a moment when this taste is muted: everything is there, but nothing nourishes. Levinas added that such a life does not by itself give meaning; meaning comes through the relation to the other, who is waiting for your response. So the way out of emptiness can begin with two small things: noticing a simple sensation — warmth, taste, light — and responding to at least one call from someone else.
emptiness.practice: Notice one simple sensation right now — the warmth of a cup, light from the window, the taste of water — and stay with it for half a minute. This is Levinas's "living from".

confusion.text: Levinas loved one strange discovery of Descartes: a thought that contains more than it can hold — "the idea of the infinite". Confusion, when the world or a person doesn't fit your ideas, is an honest state, and it is closer to this thought than it seems. This, for Levinas, is how the encounter with another person works: they always exceed my idea of them; they cannot be fully understood or predicted. The drive to explain everything and fit it into a system Levinas called the drive towards "totality". Confusion, then, is a moment when totality cracks and something larger than your schemes shows through. It is uncomfortable, but it does not mean you are lost. Perhaps you have simply met something that cannot be appropriated — and that too is knowledge.
confusion.practice: For a minute, stay in the confusion without explaining anything. Say to yourself: "This is more than I understand yet" — and simply breathe.

fatigue.text: "A lagging of oneself behind oneself" — this is what Levinas called fatigue, and he was one of the few philosophers to describe it seriously. If you are worn out, it is a real state, not a whim. In Existence and Existents (1947), he analyses fatigue and indolence not as flaws of character but as a particular relation to existence itself. In fatigue you seem unable to keep up with your own life, and being itself becomes a burden. This is a description, not a reproach. It helps to see that burnout is not a lack of will but a moment when existence feels like a load you have to drag. Levinas gives no recipe, but if we follow his thought, this heaviness is not your fault, and rest is not an escape from life but a way to find your place in it again.
fatigue.practice: Notice where in your body the fatigue is strongest, and let that part hold nothing for a minute: drop your shoulders, unclench your jaw, let your weight sink into the support.

boredom.text: "In the beginning is the relation," Martin Buber wrote in I and Thou, and this phrase may explain your boredom. Boredom can be oppressive, and it does not mean you are ungrateful or lazy. Buber distinguished two basic attitudes to the world. In the "I–It" relation we know, use and plan: the world becomes a set of objects and tasks. In the "I–Thou" relation we meet something whole — a person, a tree, a work of art — and it seems to answer us. Buber believed that we cannot live without the world of "It", but that a life lived only in it impoverishes a person. In other words, boredom is a sign that there is too much "It" around you: everything is familiar, useful, predictable, and nothing addresses you. The way out is not necessarily new entertainment — rather, letting something become a "Thou" for you.
boredom.practice: Listen to one song, or to a sound outside the window, as if it were addressing you personally — not as background but as a "Thou". A minute is enough.

quote.text: Without It man cannot live. But he who lives with It alone is not a man.
quote.author: Martin Buber

joy.text: Good food, warmth, light — in Totality and Infinity Levinas gladly lists what we live from and calls it "enjoyment" (jouissance). Your joy can be trusted: for all the rigour of his ethics, he did not devalue it. For him this is not selfishness to be ashamed of but a necessary way of being yourself, of feeling your independence and happiness. But the thought goes further: in Otherwise than Being, Levinas wrote that you can truly give to another only what you yourself enjoy — like bread taken from your own mouth. Then your joy is doubly valuable: it nourishes you, and it can become a gift to another. It needs neither justification nor permission.
joy.practice: Share part of what is making you glad with someone — a treat, a song, a piece of news. Levinas believed you can only give what you yourself enjoy.

quote.text: We live from "good soup," air, light, spectacles, work, ideas, sleep…
quote.author: Emmanuel Levinas

love.text: Levinas gave the lectures Time and the Other in 1947, and one of his thoughts on love sounds surprising: in love the other remains a mystery, and the relationship never becomes possession. Your tenderness is one of the strongest responses to another person. Even the caress, as he described it, seeks not what is already known but what keeps slipping away, what is still to come. Buber, in I and Thou, stressed that love is not simply a feeling inside a person but something that happens between people when an "I" addresses a "Thou". If so, your tenderness is not a wish to appropriate but a readiness to meet someone who can never be fully known. This makes love not poorer but more alive: there is always room in it for surprise.
love.practice: Look at someone you love today as if seeing them for the first time, and notice one thing that surprises you. Levinas would say: they are more than you know about them.

quote.text: Feelings dwell in man; but man dwells in his love.
quote.author: Martin Buber

gratitude.text: "Man becomes an I through a Thou," Buber wrote in I and Thou. Gratitude is precisely the warm feeling in which you acknowledge that you received something that did not come from yourself. For Buber and Levinas this acknowledgement runs very deep: a person does not begin with themselves at all. Buber, in I and Thou, held that relation comes first: we become ourselves by answering another's address. Levinas saw the same dependence but stressed its ethical side: in Totality and Infinity the other comes to me not as a partner in a deal but as someone who surpasses me and teaches me something. In this light, gratitude is not a debt to be repaid as quickly as possible but joy at not being alone in your existence. You can simply live it, without turning it into a calculation.
gratitude.practice: Name one person thanks to whom you became who you are, and thank them — in person, by message or in your mind, addressing them directly as "you".

quote.text: In the beginning is the relation.
quote.author: Martin Buber

hope.text: The future, Levinas said in Time and the Other, comes to us from outside, unexpectedly, like another person — it cannot be foreseen or planned. Hope matters most when the future is unclear, and this thought can support it. So time, for Levinas, is above all a relation to the other. So hope does not have to rest on a confident forecast. It can be an openness to what you cannot yet imagine: an encounter, a word, help, a turn of events that could not be invented in advance. If it is hard right now to rely only on yourself, hope can live in the fact that you do not face the future alone.
hope.practice: Recall a time when something good came into your life unexpectedly, through another person. Tell this story to someone — as a reminder that the future is not exhausted by forecasts.

nostalgia.text: Odysseus and Abraham are the two heroes Levinas used, in "The Trace of the Other" (1963), to explain two ways of living: one keeps returning home to Ithaca, the other leaves for ever for an unknown land. Nostalgia, in which love for what once was lives on, is the feeling of Odysseus, and it is natural. But Levinas saw another path too. True desire, for Levinas, is not a longing to return but a movement towards the other, towards what was never yours. This does not make nostalgia bad: remembering home is human. But its warmth can be not only a look backward but also the strength with which you go to meet what is new.
nostalgia.practice: Today, walk for five minutes along a route that is new to you, and take one warm memory with you — like Abraham, who leaves carrying what he loves.

craving.text: "Riveted" is the word the young Levinas used, in On Escape (1935), for the feeling that you cannot rest from your own existence. An acute "I want it right now" can be almost unbearable, and there is no need to be ashamed of it. Pleasure, he wrote, promises such an exit, but the promise proves deceptive: the moment passes, and the person is alone with themselves again — often with an even greater weight. This means a craving is not a whim but a very human wish to be free, even briefly, of the burden of being yourself. Levinas saw the real way beyond oneself not in a substance or a habit but in the relation to the Other. The wave of craving rises and falls — and you can wait it out, remembering what it is really looking for.
craving.practice: When the wave of craving rises, feel your feet on the floor and ask: "What in me do I want to rest from right now?" Name it aloud and keep breathing until the wave begins to fall.

addiction.text: Buber distinguished the "I–It" relation, where we deal with things and means, from "I–Thou", where we meet the other whole. In his language, a life long organised around one thing is a world in which a single "It" has eclipsed almost every "Thou". It is a heavy and lonely circle, and it does not make you a bad person. In Totality and Infinity (1961), Levinas said that a person lives "from" things — food, light, work — and there is nothing wrong in that; but real openness begins where the face of another person appears. The way out of the circle, by this logic, lies not through self-punishment but through the return of encounters.
addiction.practice: Call or meet one person with whom you are a "Thou", not a function. Such encounters also happen in mutual-help groups, where others know this circle from the inside.

hangover.text: Nausea and shame are two feelings Levinas described with remarkable precision in On Escape (1935), as if he had such a morning in mind. The morning after — with anxiety and gaps in memory — is hard, and right now you are allowed to be gentle with yourself. Nausea, for him, is a state in which you cannot get away from yourself: body and existence press down on you entirely. Shame is the experience of being seen and unable to hide, even from yourself. Levinas stressed that shame concerns not so much a deed as our very nakedness and vulnerability. In other words, your morning shame is not a final verdict but an experience of human fragility that everyone shares. You can treat it gently: first come back into your body, and sort through yesterday later.
hangover.practice: Place a palm on your chest or belly and take a few slow out-breaths. Tell yourself: "Right now I feel bad, and it will pass." The body first; yesterday later.

euphoria.text: Light, air, food, ideas — in Totality and Infinity (1961), Levinas called the way we live from all this "enjoyment", and saw real, innocent happiness in it. A sudden rush, when everything seems possible, is a vivid experience, and you can simply enjoy it. He did not consider it something lower. But he noticed something else too: enjoyment lives in the moment and does not know what tomorrow will bring. Then euphoria is one of the fullest forms of such enjoyment, and there is no guilt in it. What gives it depth, for Levinas, is encounter: joy becomes sturdier when it can be shared with another person rather than only lived inside.
euphoria.practice: Tell someone in one sentence what has lifted you up like this. For Levinas, joy grows sturdier when it is addressed to another.

crash.text: Levinas soberly observed that enjoyment comes with no guarantees. A sharp drop after a celebration, a success or a bright evening can be very hard, and it is not your fault. In Totality and Infinity (1961), he wrote that the enjoyment we live from always comes without guarantees: its "future" is uncertain, and the joy of the moment does not protect us from what comes next. In Existence and Existents (1947), he carefully described fatigue as a state in which existence suddenly becomes heavy, like a burden. If so, the "comedown" is not a sign that something is wrong with you but the flip side of the very capacity for joy. Levinas did not suggest running from this heaviness; he pointed to where to look for support: not in the next high, but in the relation with another.
crash.practice: Send one person a short message for no reason — just to be in touch. Levinas looked for support not in the next high but in another person.

panic.text: Standing, leaning on something, taking a place — for Levinas these are not trifles but where consciousness begins. A wave of panic is one of the most frightening experiences: it feels as if the ground is slipping from under your feet. In Existence and Existents (1947), Levinas described a state he called the "il y a" — "there is": impersonal being in which there is no one and nothing definite, only the hum of existence. He said it evokes not anxiety but "horror". But in the same book Levinas described how a person emerges from this hum: through "position" — through the body taking a place, resting on the ground, finding a "base". In this light, pressing your feet against the floor is no small thing but a literal return of your place to you. Such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes.
panic.practice: Take your place, as Levinas put it: press your feet into the floor, feel where the chair holds you, and make the out-breath longer than the in-breath. Name three objects around you aloud — you are here.

dread.text: Levinas argued with his teacher Heidegger about the main thing: where to look for meaning — in the face of your own death, or in the face of another person? The question "what is it all for?" and dread before finitude are a very deep experience, and it is hard to be alone with them. In his lectures Time and the Other (1947), Levinas wrote that death is not something we can understand or "take on": it is a mystery beyond our powers. Meaning, for Levinas, comes not from facing your own finitude but from meeting another person — their "face", which addresses me and needs me. So the question "what for?" can be answered not with a theory but with a relationship: someone needs me, and I need someone. The abyss does not disappear, but another person appears in it.
dread.practice: Find a person or creature who may need you today — a neighbour, a friend, a cat, a plant — and do something very small for them.

fomo.text: Levinas called it "totality" when all people are fitted into one system, compared and ranked — a social media feed would probably have struck him as the perfect example. It only sharpens the feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives and you are not where you should be. Comparison is just such a small totality: me and others as points on one scale. But for Levinas the real other cannot be reduced to any scale: their "face" is always more than whatever can be shown of them. The same is true of you: your life is not an item in a common ranking. Buber would add that a feed shows people as "It" — pictures — while encounter happens only with a "Thou". Wherever you truly meet someone, you are already "where you should be".
fomo.practice: Put your phone away and for two minutes simply be where you are — with whoever is near, or with the silence. Say to yourself: "Here I am, here."

sleepless.text: Levinas made philosophy out of two simple words, "can't sleep": in Existence and Existents (1947) he described a vigil without an object, when impersonal being itself, the "il y a", won't let you go. Night hours when thoughts give you no peace can be painfully lonely. Levinas knew such nights and described them more precisely than most. For Levinas, sleep is the possibility of "laying yourself down", of finding support and shelter. This means insomnia is not your failure but a state everyone knows, in which it is hard to find your place. And he saw the way out not in forcing yourself to sleep but in finding support again — your body, the bed, your place.
sleepless.practice: Feel where your body touches the bed: heels, back, the back of your head. Notice each point of support in turn without trying to fall asleep — simply take your place.

betrayal.text: "The exalted melancholy of our fate" — this is what Buber called the fact that every "Thou" sooner or later becomes an "It": even the closest person sometimes turns, for us, into an object, a means, a function. Betrayal hurts especially because it comes from where you were open. Betrayal can be seen as the moment when you suddenly found yourself to be not a "Thou" for the other but an "It". Levinas would add that the face of the other is always vulnerable, and that is exactly why yours is open too: to be capable of trust is to be capable of being wounded. In other words, your pain is not evidence of naivety but confirmation that you truly lived in the relationship.
betrayal.practice: Write down which part of yourself you were open to this person with. It is yours, and it does not disappear with the betrayal.

jealousy.text: The other can never be fully understood, appropriated or held on to — Levinas saw this not as love's misfortune but as its condition. Jealousy is agonising: the fear of losing someone squeezes everything inside. The other is not part of me or my extension; in love we meet precisely this unfathomability. Then jealousy can be understood as a painful collision with the fact that the other always remains other — they have a depth of their own to which we have no access. This does not make you a bad person: it is how the strength of your attachment shows itself. But Levinas also offers consolation: it is exactly because the other cannot be appropriated that the encounter with them is alive. If they could be held completely, it would no longer be love but the possession of a thing.
jealousy.practice: Write down one thing about this person that you love precisely because it doesn't depend on you.

quote.text: The relationship with the other is a relationship with a Mystery.
quote.author: Emmanuel Levinas

resentment.text: In his Talmudic Readings (1968), Levinas examined an old text: offences against God are forgiven on the Day of Atonement, but offences against a person only when the offender has gone to the one they wronged. If a long-held grievance is with you, you were once truly hurt. Levinas gave this great importance: harm done to a person is real harm, and it cannot be erased in the abstract. If so, your grievance is legitimate: it remembers that you were treated unjustly. No one has the right to demand quick forgiveness from you. But you can ask how to carry this memory so that it does not take away your capacity for new encounters.
resentment.practice: Slowly say aloud the words from the text Levinas studied: "Offences against a person are forgiven only when the offender has gone to the one they wronged." Stay for a minute with the fact that your grievance is legitimate.

heartbreak.text: Levinas did not believe in the myth of two halves: in his lectures Time and the Other (1947), love is not fusion but a relation with someone who always slips away. A break-up can feel like a wound that won't close. The beloved never becomes entirely "mine" — and in this lie both the depth of love and its fragility. In this light, a break-up is a painful confirmation that the other was always other: free, separate. This does not cancel the pain or make the past unreal: the encounter happened, and it was genuine. Buber wrote that real relationships live "between" people. What was between you has already happened, and it cannot be undone — even now, when you are apart.
heartbreak.practice: Write down one moment from this relationship when you truly met. It happened, and it cannot be undone.

quote.text: The pathos of love consists in an insurmountable duality of beings.
quote.author: Emmanuel Levinas

impostor.text: Who gave you the right to be here? Levinas would answer: the one who addressed you. The fear of being found out at any moment often torments those who are doing perfectly well. For Buber, a person does not "make themselves" alone: they become themselves in relationships, in encounter with another. For Levinas, my uniqueness is born not from achievements but from the fact that I am addressed and I answer: "Here I am." No one can answer in my place. So impostor syndrome rests on a false premise: that your right to be here has to be earned by flawlessness. But you are here because you were addressed and you responded. That cannot be "exposed": a response is not a mask but who you already are.
impostor.practice: Recall who came to you with a request this week and how you answered. Silently repeat: "Here I am" — that is your place.

quote.text: Through the Thou a man becomes I.
quote.author: Martin Buber

self_hatred.text: In Totality and Infinity (1961), Levinas argued against the "judgement of history" — a verdict passed on a person in absentia, as if they were not in the room. A living face, he said, cannot be reduced to a verdict. If your inner voice is merciless, living with it is very hard, and you deserve gentleness. The inner critic resembles such a trial in absentia: it talks about you in the third person, lists, sums up. But for Levinas a person is always more than any summary of them. Buber would say that the critic treats you as an "It", an object to be fixed. This means you can decline the critic's verdict — not by arguing with it, but by reminding yourself that you are not an object but someone who can be addressed as "you".
self_hatred.practice: Imagine the critic has to say its sentence to your face — looking you in the eye, addressing you as "you". Notice how it changes when the trial in absentia becomes an encounter.

helplessness.text: When nothing can be changed, is anything left? Levinas answered: a response is left. Powerlessness is a very heavy feeling, and it deserves to be taken seriously. Levinas wrote a great deal about passivity and vulnerability. In Otherwise than Being (1974), he speaks of "sensibility" as the capacity to be affected, to be woundable — and sees in it not weakness but the foundation of humanity. For him a person is defined not only by what they can do but also by how they can respond. Even when you cannot change the situation, you can say "here I am" — be present, look, not turn away. In other words, helplessness is not your absence but a place where you are vulnerable together with others. And in that place a small but real response is still possible.
helplessness.practice: Stay for a minute beside what you cannot change — without turning away and without doing anything. Say to yourself: "Here I am." Sometimes presence is already a response.

procrastination.text: Levinas is perhaps the only major philosopher to have given laziness a serious analysis — in Existence and Existents (1947). When you just can't get started, it is easy to call yourself lazy, but his view is gentler. Levinas wrote that indolence is not simply unwillingness to work but a recoil before beginning itself: to begin is to take on the burden of existence, to enter an action that will demand all of you. So for Levinas indolence is linked to weariness with being, not to bad character. Then "I can't start" is a natural response to the weight of the first step. Hence the relief: you don't have to begin heroically. You can begin with something so small that it barely feels like a beginning.
procrastination.practice: Do the tiniest action on the task — open the file, put the thing you need on the desk — and only that. Levinas would say: a beginning doesn't have to be heroic.

uprooted.text: Kaunas, Strasbourg, Freiburg, Paris — Levinas walked the emigrant's road himself and knew what it means to lose a familiar world. When the ground goes from under your feet, it is a deep and real loss. In his essay "Heidegger, Gagarin and Us" (1961), he argued against the cult of "roots" and "place": for him a human being is not a plant, and their dignity does not depend on the soil they grew in. He liked to contrast Odysseus, who is always trying to return home, with Abraham, who sets out into the unknown. Then being cut off from home is painful, but it is not a loss of self. Your humanity, for Levinas, lives not in a place but in your relationships with people, and it moves with you.
uprooted.practice: Today, truly greet one person in the new place — a neighbour, a shop assistant, a colleague — looking at their face. For Levinas, humanity lives not in soil but in encounters.

overload.text: In Otherwise than Being (1974), Levinas distinguished "the said" — facts, content, information — from "the saying": the very act of one person addressing another. An endless stream of notifications wears you out, and it is clear why: there is so much of the first and almost none of the second — streams of text in which no one truly addresses you. You are not obliged to keep up with it. Buber would speak of the world of "It", where everything is objects and data. If so, feed fatigue is not your inability to "keep up" but a hunger for real address. What helps is not a new way to keep up with everything but a small step out of the stream towards a living voice.
overload.practice: Put the feed away and call one person not "on business" but simply to hear their voice. This is saying without the said.

unreality.text: A world that has lost its shapes and meanings, with only a dull presence left in which there is no "I" — Levinas called this the "il y a", the impersonal "there is". If everything around you, or you yourself, feels somehow not quite real, it is frightening and lonely, and it deserves care. But he also pointed to what brings us back to reality — above all, another person's face: their gaze and voice address us, and we turn out to be someone. Buber would say that reality is born in encounter. Perhaps reality returns not through reflection but through contact.
unreality.practice: Hear a living voice — call someone close or listen to a person near you — and notice its timbre. Buber would say: reality is born in encounter.

awe.text: Buber insisted that even a tree can be met as a "Thou" — not examined but met whole. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare experience, and you can simply let it fill you. In Totality and Infinity (1961), Levinas drew on Descartes' thought of the "idea of the infinite": we have a thought that holds more than it can hold. For Levinas this experience — when something surpasses us and does not fit into our understanding — happens above all in the encounter with another person, but an echo of it is present in any awe. In this light, awe is the moment when the world stops being "It" and becomes "Thou" again. Such a moment needs nothing added to it.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with what stirred your awe, as if it were looking at you just as you are looking at it.

relief.text: Being "riveted" to yourself and your worries — this is how Levinas, in On Escape (1935), described the weight a person longs to be even a little free of. Relief, when something heavy finally lets go, is a wonderful feeling and worth noticing. So relief is that rare moment when the weight really lifts and you can breathe. Often it comes not on its own but through another — through a word, help, a hug, news of someone close. Levinas believed that it is the other who leads us beyond ourselves. So relief is a good occasion to remember who or what helped, and perhaps to say so.
relief.practice: Take a long out-breath and ask yourself: who helped this happen? If someone did, tell them today, even in a single word.

calm.text: In Totality and Infinity (1961), Levinas wrote a great deal about "home" — not walls but a place where you can gather yourself, rest from the pressure of the world, and go out from to meet others. Calm is a precious state; you can simply be in it. Levinas linked home with "gentleness" — an atmosphere of hospitality in which a person feels welcomed. This means calm is the experience of such a home, even if it lasts a minute and is found not in an apartment but in you. Levinas stressed that home is also precious because you can invite another into it. But first you can simply be in it yourself.
calm.practice: Notice what around you right now creates a sense of home — a light, a sound, an object — and silently thank it.

inspiration.text: Not only artists know this word: in Otherwise than Being (1974) Levinas used "inspiration" for the very depth of the human soul. The moment when a thought or image seems to arrive from outside and you want to create is one of the best sides of life. For him a person is not a closed fortress: "the other-in-the-same" lives in us, and we breathe what does not come from us. Inspiration is the experience of being open to something larger than yourself. Buber said something similar about creation: a form awaits encounter and addresses the artist, and the artist answers. In other words, inspiration is neither an achievement nor an accident but a response to being addressed. You can simply respond.
inspiration.practice: Write down what has just come as an answer to the question "What is addressing me right now?" — without edits.

schadenfreude.text: Buber distinguished two relations to a person: meeting them whole — "I–Thou" — and "I–It", when they become a figure in our calculations. In the "It" mode a rival turns into a line on the scoreboard, and their loss seems like our point. Hence schadenfreude, embarrassing to admit even to yourself, though in itself it says little about who you are. Levinas would call this the gaze of "totality" — a gaze that inscribes the other into its own system. But once you see a "face" in the same person — someone alive and vulnerable, for whom something has also collapsed — schadenfreude usually weakens by itself. There is no need to punish yourself; it is enough to notice this shift.
schadenfreude.practice: For a minute, picture this person not as a rival but at home in the evening after their failure. Notice what has changed in your feeling.

contempt.text: The face of the other, for Levinas, speaks to us both from defencelessness and from a "height" — as someone who cannot be reduced to our assessment. Contempt is looking down, when the other seems petty and unworthy; sometimes it has grounds, and it does not make you a bad person. Contempt tries to turn this picture upside down: to put yourself above and stop listening. Following Levinas's thought, contempt often protects against something — disappointment, hurt, the need to recognise in the other the same vulnerability as in yourself. You need not fight it; you can ask: what exactly do I stop hearing when I feel contempt?
contempt.practice: Recall how this person looked in a moment of tiredness or bewilderment. Stay with that face for a minute and ask: what do I stop seeing when I feel contempt?

quote.text: The face is what one cannot kill, or at least it is that whose meaning consists in saying: "thou shalt not kill."
quote.author: Emmanuel Levinas

disgust.text: In On Escape (1935), three years before Sartre's Nausea, Levinas described nausea as a philosophical experience: the impossibility of getting rid of yourself, being "riveted" to your own existence. Disgust is a strong bodily feeling, directed at people, a situation, sometimes at yourself, and it does not make you bad. Then self-disgust is especially agonising: there is nowhere to step away from it. Later Levinas saw the way out not in sinking further into yourself but in turning towards another person, who leads you out of confinement. Disgust, then, is a signal that the space has become too cramped, and what widens it is not straining against yourself but connection.
disgust.practice: If the disgust is directed at yourself, send someone one simple, warm message. Levinas looked for the way out of confinement in turning towards another.

revenge.text: What is justice, if not revenge? Levinas answered: what appears when a "third party" enters the relationship between two. The wish for revenge grows out of a real wound: you were treated unjustly, and your soul demands an answer. The feeling is understandable, and at its root lies an important truth: injustice should not go without consequences. Levinas distinguished ethics — the responsibility I bear before the face of a particular other — from justice, which arises when a "third party" enters the relationship: other people who must also be taken into account. Justice, for Levinas, requires comparison, weighing, courts, institutions — everything personal retribution cannot provide. If so, the wish for revenge can be understood as a demand for justice looking for the right form. There is no need to be ashamed of it; what matters is not letting it turn you into someone you don't want to be.
revenge.practice: Write down what kind of justice you would need: an admission of guilt, an apology, amends, protection. This helps tell a need for justice apart from a wish to cause pain.

anger_at_loved.text: In 1957 Martin Buber went on stage for a public dialogue with the psychologist Carl Rogers and distinguished there between "accepting" another and "confirming" them. Anger at those close to you can be scorching, and shame comes after it — and this distinction can help. To confirm someone close is to acknowledge them whole, to see who they could become; and at the same time, Buber said, one can struggle against what is happening in them now. In this light, anger does not contradict love: it can be part of a real relationship in which the other matters to you rather than leaving you indifferent. Indifference would be much further from love than anger. What matters is only not to pour the anger out on the other and not to hide it from yourself, but to find words for it, addressed to them as a "Thou".
anger_at_loved.practice: When the anger subsides, say one sentence addressed directly to your loved one: "I'm angry because I see what our relationship could be…" — and finish it.

ambivalence.text: "Alterity" is one of Levinas's key words: another person is always other; they cannot be fully understood, appropriated or fitted into one picture. Loving someone and not being able to stand them at the same time is exhausting, but it is a very human state. That is why someone close to us inevitably both draws us and resists us — does not match our expectations. Mixed feelings are, in a sense, an honest response to this otherness. Buber understood love not as a feeling that "lives" in me but as a relation of responsibility for another. So you do not have to untangle all your feelings first in order to love: love can hold both irritation and tenderness, remaining a choice to care.
ambivalence.practice: Do one small thing for this person out of care — without waiting for your feelings to untangle. Buber understood love as responsibility, not as a mood.

quote.text: Love is responsibility of an I for a Thou.
quote.author: Martin Buber

guilty_relief.text: Infinite responsibility for the other is Levinas's central thought, and it may seem that such an ethics demands carrying the load without end. Relief after a break-up, the death of someone close, or long care for someone seriously ill often brings shame: how can I feel lighter? But in Otherwise than Being (1974), he added something important: thanks to "the third party", thanks to justice, I too turn out to be "an other for others" — someone who needs to be cared for. Your exhaustion has weight too. This means relief is not a betrayal of love but a sign of how long you carried an enormous responsibility. The breath out after it does not cancel the fact that you were there.
guilty_relief.practice: Take one long out-breath and tell yourself: "I too am an other for others — and I too may be cared for." Stay with this for a minute.

indifference.text: Levinas loved the play on words "non-indifference": the other affects us before we have had time to feel anything. So when there is silence inside where something "should" move you, it is frightening — but it does not mean you are heartless. This being-affected, for Levinas, lives deeper than emotions, in "sensibility" as vulnerability. In other words, the absence of feeling on the surface does not mean the absence of connection: sometimes the psyche is simply tired, overloaded or protecting itself. In Existence and Existents, Levinas described fatigue as a state in which existence seems to lag behind itself. You don't need to force yourself to feel "the right way"; you can simply stay close — with attention, with action — and the feeling may come later.
indifference.practice: If the feeling doesn't come, do one small thing for someone near you: a question, some help, attention. Notice what happens inside afterwards.

escape.text: On Escape is the title of one of Levinas's first essays (1935), and it is about that very wish to drop everything — work, city, role — and go wherever the road leads. This is often how a life that has become too cramped speaks. He described the need to go beyond one's own limits, the painful "riveted" state of being bound to one's existence, and noticed that this need cannot be satisfied by a simple change of scene: we take ourselves along. Later he saw the real "way out" in the relation to another person. In The Way of Man, Buber retold a Hasidic tale about a poor man who searched for treasure in a distant capital and found it under the stove of his own house. This is not an argument about whether to leave or not. Then the wish to escape deserves to be heard: it speaks of a real confinement, and part of the answer may be closer than it seems.
escape.practice: Retell to yourself the tale Buber loved: a poor man searched for treasure in a distant capital and found it under the stove of his own house. Look around: what is precious right here?

forbidden_attraction.text: Levinas distinguished "need" from "desire" — and the distinction unexpectedly sheds light on attraction to someone who is "off-limits". Such a feeling can be embarrassing and frightening, but in itself it decides nothing for you and says nothing about what kind of person you are. A need can be satisfied — with bread, rest, possession. "Metaphysical desire", for Levinas, is different: it reaches towards what surpasses us and is never fully appropriated. In his lectures Time and the Other (1947), he described love as a relation to mystery: it seeks what keeps slipping away. If so, unavailability can be part of the attraction itself — what draws you to the other is precisely their otherness. You can explore this feeling without rushing either to condemn yourself or to decide anything.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Go for a five-minute walk and let this feeling simply walk beside you, without judging it or deciding anything. Ask yourself: what part of my own life is this mystery calling me to?

social_anxiety.text: To be or to seem — Martin Buber considered this the main choice in any conversation. Fear of people and their judgement makes simple things hard: starting a conversation, walking into a room, making a call. In his essay "Elements of the Interhuman" (1953), he distinguished "being" from "seeming": a person can live from who they are, or from how they want to appear. Buber believed that everyone knows the urge to seem, and it is not a vice in itself, but it is exactly what gets in the way of genuine encounter and takes a great deal of energy. Levinas would add that meeting another is not showing yourself but answering their address. In this light, relief comes when attention shifts from "how do I look" to "who is in front of me and what are they saying". You don't need to be brilliant; it is enough to be present.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, allow yourself one simple, unrehearsed sentence. Notice what happens when you are not trying to seem.

uncertainty.text: Levinas likened the future to another person: neither can be fully understood or appropriated in advance. Uncertainty is exhausting — it is unclear what will happen, and there is nothing to lean on — and wanting to know in advance is natural. In his lectures Time and the Other (1947), Levinas gave an unexpected definition of the future: the future is what cannot be grasped, what comes to us from outside and escapes our control. For Levinas this is not only a threat but also a source of the new: if the future were known, there would be nothing truly other in it. So uncertainty is the other side of life's openness. It is easier to bear not alone but alongside people who don't know either.
uncertainty.practice: Talk with someone about what neither of you knows about the future. Notice how the uncertainty changes when it is shared.

waiting.text: Levinas valued "patience" as a particular form of openness: what comes from the other cannot be hurried or forced. Waiting for an answer, results, news stretches time and keeps you from living, especially when the outcome does not depend on you. It is hard, and there is no need to pretend you don't care. Buber wrote something similar about encounter: it cannot be obtained by effort; it comes as a gift. This does not mean waiting should be pleasant. But you can see in waiting not only helplessness but also an honest acknowledgement: the world and other people are not an extension of our will. You can surround the waiting with care for yourself, without demanding calm of yourself.
waiting.practice: While you wait, do one kind thing for yourself or for someone else — not to distract yourself, but so that the time of waiting is also a time of living.

quote.text: The Thou meets me through grace — it is not found by seeking.
quote.author: Martin Buber

regret.text: "Where are you?" — Buber opens The Way of Man with this question of God to Adam: not to catch him out, but so that the person sees for himself where he has ended up. Regret over what you did or didn't do can come back again and again, and it says that something mattered to you. In his essay "Guilt and Guilt Feelings" (1957), Martin Buber distinguished fruitless self-torment from "existential guilt" — the honest acknowledgement that you violated or missed something in your relationships with people and the world. Such guilt, for Buber, is not a verdict but the beginning of a path: to shed light on what happened, to remain the one who answers for it, and where possible to restore the broken connection — if not with the same person, then with the world. This means regret is not a reason to punish yourself but an invitation to respond. The past cannot be changed, but what you make of it now can.
regret.practice: Ask yourself Buber's question, "Where are you?", and answer honestly in one sentence: where are you now in this story? Then consider whether there is a small step that could restore the broken connection.

longing.text: A "Thou" cannot be had like a thing, Buber wrote — one can only stand in relation with it. Longing for a particular person can be almost physical: you miss their voice, their face, their presence. It is the natural price of a real bond. Levinas believed that another person is never exhausted by our idea of them: they are always more than we know about them. That is why no memory or photograph can replace a living face — and why longing is so sharp. In other words, longing is also a form of relationship: you remain turned towards this person even when they are not near. Longing reminds you that this relationship is alive. You can live it as faithfulness to an encounter that was, and remains, part of you.
longing.practice: Say one sentence — aloud or in a whisper — addressed directly to this person, as "you". Notice what you feel.

quote.text: Whoever says You does not have something; he has nothing. But he stands in relation.
quote.author: Martin Buber

world_pain.text: For Levinas, the suffering of another addresses us before any theory. If pain for the world — for wars, injustice, hard news — weighs on you so much that it is hard to live an ordinary life, it speaks of your capacity to respond. In his essay "Useless Suffering" (1982), he wrote that suffering in itself is meaningless, and that only a response — the help, the care of another — gives it a human dimension. But Levinas also spoke of "the third party": there are many people, and responsibility has to be measured and shared out, turning it into justice, which is larger than any one person. Then you are not obliged to carry the whole world alone. You can respond where you are: to a particular person near you.
world_pain.practice: Choose one particular face — a person near you, or those who help others — and take a small step towards them. Then allow yourself rest.

rejection.text: An "I–Thou" encounter, Buber wrote, cannot be forced: it takes two, and each is free in it. Rejection hurts as if it were not a request that was turned down but you as a whole, and this pain is natural. Levinas stressed the same freedom in his own way: another person is not an extension of our wishes; their "otherness" includes the right to say "no". It hurts, but this freedom is also what makes an encounter real: if the other could not refuse, their "yes" would mean nothing. If so, a refusal passes no verdict on your worth; it speaks of the other's freedom and of the fact that this encounter did not come together. You can still be a "Thou" for other people, and they for you.
rejection.practice: Get in touch today with one person for whom you are truly "you" — just to talk. Buber would say: encounter goes on wherever it is possible.

abandonment.text: "Here I am," says the one who answers another's call in Levinas; the fear of abandonment is the fear that no one will answer your own call. It can run very deep: it seems that without the other your support will vanish. In his early works Levinas described the "il y a" — the impersonal "there is", dull faceless being in which a person feels utterly alone. It is another person, for Levinas, who pulls us out of this solitude — which is why the fear of losing someone close is so strong: it touches the very foundation. But in Totality and Infinity Levinas also wrote about "dwelling" — a home where a person can gather themselves and rest — and linked it to the experience of hospitality, of having once been welcomed. In this light, the experience of having been welcomed stays with you, even when someone leaves.
abandonment.practice: Recall a place or a person with whom you felt welcomed. Name the feeling in three words and stay with it for a minute.

unrequited.text: Loving without first demanding reciprocity — Levinas saw nothing foolish or humiliating in it. Unrequited love hurts badly: the feeling is there, but there is no answer — yet that does not make it any less real. Your love was not a deal that "didn't pay off". But Levinas insisted just as much on the otherness of the other: to love a person is to recognise their freedom, including the freedom not to respond. And Buber wrote that a living relationship is mutual — which is why it hurts so much without an answer: the encounter remained unfinished. So you can both value your feeling and take care of yourself: not demanding an answer from the other, and not demanding that you stop loving at once.
unrequited.practice: Jot down what your love has given you yourself: which sides of yourself you discovered in it. That remains yours.

humiliation.text: Defenceless and at the same time demanding respect — this is how Levinas described the human face. Humiliation is one of the hardest experiences: it feels as if your dignity has been taken from you, often in front of others. Levinas would say: your face has not stopped being a face. Humiliation tries to reduce you to an object — to an "It", Buber would say — to a thing that can be appraised and discarded. But for Levinas the face can never be entirely turned into a thing: it always remains more than any attempt to belittle it. This means humiliation speaks of the act of the one who humiliated, not of your essence. The pain is real, but you don't have to accept the verdict.
humiliation.practice: Divide a sheet into two columns: "what was done to me" and "who I am". In the second, write down what has stayed unchanged.

body_shame.text: "The best way of encountering the Other is not even to notice the colour of his eyes," Levinas said in the conversations Ethics and Infinity (1982). If the mirror has turned into an exam, it is exhausting, and you are not alone in this. Levinas distinguished the "face" from appearance. The face, for Levinas, is not a set of features that can be rated but the very way a person addresses another: their presence, voice, vulnerability. And in Totality and Infinity, Levinas described the body as that by which we "live from" the world: enjoying warmth, food, light. In other words, the body is not a picture to be examined but your way of being in the world and with others. The people who love you meet you, not your reflection.
body_shame.practice: Think of someone dear to you. What do you value in them? Notice how much of it has nothing to do with appearance — and try it on yourself.

quote.text: The best way of encountering the Other is not even to notice the color of his eyes!
quote.author: Emmanuel Levinas

illness.text: Levinas wrote about suffering without comforting illusions — which is why he is worth reading when you are ill. When the body lets you down — illness, pain, weakness — life changes, and fear, irritation and sadness are natural here. In his lectures Time and the Other, he said that in physical pain a person is as if pressed against their own existence, with nowhere to retreat. And in his essay "Useless Suffering" (1982), he wrote that suffering in itself carries no higher meaning — which means you don't have to force yourself to draw a lesson from it. Meaning, for Levinas, appears in relation: when another responds to your pain — and when you allow them to. Then illness is neither your fault nor a test you have to "pass correctly". You can allow yourself to accept help.
illness.practice: Ask someone for a small bit of help — or simply tell them how you feel. Notice what happens when your pain is shared.

pride.text: Levinas, a strict philosopher of responsibility, nevertheless defended "enjoyment": a person lives "from" the world — from work, food, light, ideas — and delights in it. Pride in what you have done is a good, well-earned feeling, and there is no need to hide it. For him such joy is not selfishness but the foundation of a separate "I", which can then give to others. In The Way of Man According to the Teaching of Hasidism (1948), Buber wrote that every person brings something new into the world, something that has never existed before, and that their task is to unfold precisely this. If so, your pride is joy at having made something of your own. It deserves to be enjoyed and perhaps shared with someone who will be glad for you.
pride.practice: Read Buber's words aloud: "Every person brings something new into the world, something that has never existed before." Consider what new thing you have brought into the world with this work.

melancholy.text: Every "Thou" becomes part of the everyday world again — Buber wrote about this without bitterness, as a quiet truth of the human lot. Bright sadness, in which sorrow is mixed with tenderness towards the world, doesn't need fixing. But he also believed that encounter can happen again, and that the very memory of it changes us. Levinas would add that time is not simply a series of losses but an openness to what is still to come, to the other. In this light, bright sadness is the feeling of someone who knows the value of encounters and does not turn away from their fleetingness. You can live it unhurriedly, like quiet music, and perhaps remember whom you would like to share it with.
melancholy.practice: Recall one encounter — with a person, a place, a book — that was a "Thou" for you. Stay with the memory for a minute without trying to hold on to it.

quote.text: This is the exalted melancholy of our fate, that every Thou in our world must become an It.
quote.author: Martin Buber
